conversation.content: How can I compare the metrics for different periods?

To compare metrics for different periods, you can use the time period control available in the metrics interface. This allows you to select specific time frames such as a day, week, month, or quarter, and the data points on the graphs adjust accordingly. You can also create custom time periods. Additionally, metrics can be viewed for predefined periods like 7, 15, 30, 60, or 90 days. The graphs and aggregate values can be adjusted to reflect the selected time period, enabling you to compare metrics across different time frames effectively.
some example of alerts

Examples of alerts include app-level alerts, worker node alerts, zone alerts, cluster alerts, account alerts, and block storage for VPC alerts. Additionally, presence alerts notify when the number of events or logs exceeds expectations, while absence alerts trigger when the number of events or logs falls below expectations. Alerts can be configured with specific conditions, notification channels, and severity levels to monitor infrastructure, applications, and IBM Cloud services.
weak understanding metrics

Weak understanding metrics refer to the number of individual messages that the assistant did not fully comprehend. To improve weak understanding, analyze the Analytics tab to identify areas for improvement. Use metrics to find patterns or common issues in user interactions. Test alternative approaches by creating different versions of the assistant and compare their performance. Refine the assistant's dialog skill based on the insights gained from the logs and metrics. Regularly monitor and update the assistant to enhance its understanding and effectiveness.
those conversations are monitored?

The previous conversations are monitored to improve how the assistant understands and responds to user requests. The Conversations page provides a history of interactions, allowing you to analyze user inputs, actions, and topics. You can filter and explore specific conversations to identify areas for improvement. This monitoring is part of the process to refine the assistant's performance and training data.
are they billed by the number of turns or per conversation?

The billing is managed per monthly active user per service instance. If a single user interacts with assistants hosted by different service instances that belong to the same plan, each interaction is treated as a separate use. You are billed for the user's interaction with each service instance separately. Therefore, you are billed based on the number of interactions (or monthly active users) rather than the number of turns or per conversation.

Metrics for an individual CDN are provided on the Overview tab of the customer portal for that CDN mapping. Two types of metrics are calculated from the CDN's usage: those that show the metrics over a time period as a graph, and those that are shown as aggregate values.

For metrics that display the change over a period of time as a graph, you can see three line graphs and a pie chart. The three line graphs are: Bandwidth, Hits by Mapping, and Hits by Type. They display the activity daily over the course of your specified timeframe. The graphs for Bandwidth and Hits by Mapping are single-line graphs, whereas the breakdown of Hits by Type shows a line for each of the hit types provided. The pie chart displays a regional breakdown of the bandwidth for a CDN mapping on a percentage basis.

Metrics that are shown for aggregate values include Bandwidth Usage in GB, Total Hits to the CDN Edge server, and the Hit Ratio. Hit Ratio indicates that the percentage of times content is delivered by the Edge server, not through its origin. Hit ratio currently is shown as a function of all your CDN mappings, not just the one being viewed.

By default, both the aggregate numbers and the graphs default to show metrics for the last 30 days, but you can change this through the [IBM Cloud console](https://cloud.ibm.com/). Both categories can display metrics for 7-, 15-, 30-, 60-, or 90-day periods.

Query performance in Discovery is dependent on a number of factors.



 Evaluating performance 

If you expect high simultaneous load on your application, it is important to evaluate the performance of your Discovery application. There are several dimensions commonly used to measure performance:



1. Response latency - The time it takes for Discovery to return the results of your query.



* Latency can vary depending on a number of factors, see [Factors that impact performance](https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/discovery?topic=discovery-qpperffactors) for more information.
* It is important to run tests in your production environment using a representative set of queries to determine your average latency.



2. Query rate - The number of requests that can be processed in a given time, usually measured in Queries per Second (QPS). This measure is most important when you expect high simultaneous load on your application.



* The rate that can be achieved varies based on many of the same factors as latency.
* Evaluate the query rate by using representative queries at the loads you expect to see. Remember to account for peak loads during testing.









 Factors that impact performance 

Query performance in Discovery varies, based on many factors, including plan size, query complexity, features used, and collection size and complexity.



 Plan size 

Discovery pricing plans limit the number of available documents and also provide differing ability to handle query load. The larger the plan size, the more resources that are available to handle queries. The average rate limits also vary by plan size. Upgrading your plan can improve performance. See [Discovery pricing plans](https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/discovery?topic=discovery-discovery-pricing-plans) for plans and limits.

1. Length - Longer queries most likely have poorer performance.
2. Aggregations - Aggregations are a more complex query type, with nested aggregations having the highest impact on performance.
3. Operators - Wldcarding and fuzzy matching can impact performance.

There are a number of features that enhance query results. The following features can impact performance:



1. Passage Retrieval - Passage retrieval searches within documents to find relevant snippets of text for your query. Use the passages.fields parameter to adjust which fields in the documents that passage retrieval searches. The parameter can help reduce the latency of passage retrieval when your content has many fields. For more information about passage retrieval, see [Passages](https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/discovery?topic=discovery-query-parameterspassages).
2. Relevancy Training - Relevancy training computes features for each top-level text field (fields at the same level as document_id in the JSON) in the collection. If there are many top level fields, this can cause a performance impact for a natural_language_query when using training. Reducing the number of top level fields can improve performance. This can be done via normalization or by manually editing the JSON to put fields that are not helpful to finding relevant content in a nested structure. Changing the fields used for training also has an impact on the model so you’ll need to consider both the impact to performance and accuracy of results if making this change.

To find specific conversations, you can filter the list of conversations by using the following options:  
- **Keyword**: Search by session ID or specific key terms, phrases, or words in the conversations. If searching for a session ID, enclose it in quotation marks for an exact match.  
- **Actions**: Select specific actions to review.  
- **Recognition**: Choose between recognized or unrecognized user questions.  
- **Search**: Choose between requests that initiated a search or those that produced no results.  

Additionally, you can filter by **Intents** and **Entities** to narrow down messages based on user input. For detailed exploration, click on any utterance or conversation timestamp to view the full conversation.
Is a user ID necessary to find a specific conversation?

Yes, a user ID is necessary to find a specific conversation in some contexts. For example, in the Watson Assistant service, the user_id property is used to track user interactions and associate messages with a specific user. If the user ID is not specified, the service may use a session_id or conversation_id to identify the conversation. However, the necessity of a user ID depends on the specific integration or API being used.
How to create a user ID?

To create a user ID in IBM Cloud, you typically use an IBMid, which is an email address. If a user does not have an IBMid, they can create one through the IBM website. Additionally, users can be invited to an IBM Cloud account, and their IAM ID is generated as part of their identity management. The IAM ID is used for assigning access policies and can be found in the "My user details" section under "Manage > Access (IAM)." If you need to create a user ID for a specific purpose, such as for an application or service, you may need to follow the specific steps provided by the service or application's documentation.
What is a strong password?

A strong password is one that is difficult to guess and meets specific security criteria. It should be at least 8 characters long, include a mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters. Examples of strong passwords include "T7m!p9Lq" or "P@ssw0rd!". Additionally, it should not contain personal information or be reused across accounts. Password strength can be enforced through policies and regex rules in systems like IBM Cloud's App ID dashboard.
Retention time for conversations?

The retention time for conversations in Watson Assistant depends on your service plan. For the Enterprise with Data Isolation and Premium (legacy) plans, messages are retained for the last 90 days. For the Enterprise and Plus plans, messages are retained for the last 30 days. This retention period defines how long messages are kept before they are deleted. If messages are not read by a consumer within this time, they will be missed.
Can you delete conversations?

Yes, conversations can be deleted. The "conversation" API provides actions such as "conversation.workspace.delete" to delete a workspace, "conversation.intent.delete" to delete an intent, and "conversation.example.delete" to delete a user example from an intent. Additionally, messages associated with a specific customer can be deleted by associating them with a unique Customer ID and using the "X-Watson-Metadata: customer_id" header. This process allows for the removal of user data from Watson Assistant instances.

JavaScript detections 

IBM Cloud® Internet Services (CIS) bot features include JavaScript detections. A small amount of JavaScript is injected into client devices using [Google’s Picasso fingerprinting technique](https://research.google/pubs/pub45581/). BotScoreSrc: Not Computed and a score of 0 are relevant to Picasso JavaScript Fingerprinting requests. These requests are exempt from being blocked by any firewall rules.

This detection technique gathers general data about the machines reaching CIS. Additionally, code is not injected again until its 30-minute session life expires. The Picasso script is roughly 70 KB and execution time varies by device, anywhere from 90 ms to around 500 ms.
